explanations.explanation: That's the spot, friend. John says Jesus "found men selling cattle, sheep, and doves, and money changers seated at their tables" right in the temple courts (John 2:14). Picture setting up a cash register and a pen of sheep where people came to worship. That's a lot of stuff in one courtyard.

Nice guess, but that's not where this happens. The pool is a different spot in Jerusalem, and John never puts these sellers there. The text says Jesus found them in the temple courts (John 2:14). I think the pool made sense because water makes people think of a crowd, but this crowd is in the courts.

Close in distance, but not the right place. The Mount of Olives is a hill outside the city, and John doesn't set this scene there. Jesus found the sellers and the money changers in the temple courts (John 2:14). It's one of those answers that sounds right until you check the verse.

A whip is right. John says Jesus "made a whip out of cords" (John 2:15). Notice He made it right there with what was lying around. I couldn't build anything useful from a pile of cords, so I admire the skill.

A sling is what David used against Goliath (1 Samuel 17:49), so I see where your head went. But that's a different story. Here the text says Jesus made a whip out of the cords (John 2:15). A sling needs stones, and nobody's throwing any here.

A net is made from cords, so the guess makes sense. It's just not what the verse says. John tells us Jesus "made a whip out of cords" (John 2:15). Nobody is getting caught here, they're getting driven out.

True. John says Jesus "drove all from the temple courts, both sheep and cattle" (John 2:15). The word is "all," so nobody gets to stay behind. I bet that was a LOUD moment, with hooves going everywhere.

It's actually true, friend. The text says Jesus "drove all from the temple courts, both sheep and cattle" (John 2:15). The animals went out with everyone else. It's easy to think the sellers went and the animals stayed, but the verse names the sheep and cattle right there.

explanations.answer: He pours out their coins and overturns the tables
explanations.explanation: That's it. John says Jesus "poured out the coins of the money changers and overturned their tables" (John 2:15). Coins everywhere, tables flipped. I think those money changers had a very long afternoon of picking up change.

explanations.answer: He carries their tables out to the street
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't carry anything out in this verse. John says He "poured out the coins of the money changers and overturned their tables" (John 2:15). Carrying is calm and careful, and this was neither. The tables got flipped right where they stood.

explanations.answer: He gathers their coins and folds up the tables
explanations.explanation: That's a tidy cleanup, and it's not what happened. The text says Jesus "poured out the coins of the money changers and overturned their tables" (John 2:15). He scattered the coins instead of gathering them. Nobody here is folding anything.
Marketplace is right. Jesus says, "How dare you turn My Father's house into a marketplace!" (John 2:16). He calls the temple His Father's house. That tells you how He saw the place.

A storehouse is a decent guess, since the courts had animals and coins around. But Jesus' words are, "How dare you turn My Father's house into a marketplace!" (John 2:16). He says marketplace, so that's the word to hold onto. Nothing here talks about storing things.

That one's a stretch, friend. Jesus says, "How dare you turn My Father's house into a marketplace!" (John 2:16). He doesn't say anything about a prison. The problem is the buying and selling in His Father's house.
Yes. The disciples remember it is written, "Zeal for Your house will consume Me." (John 2:17). Zeal means a burning care for something. They watch Jesus act and the verse comes to their minds.

Rest is a good Bible theme, but it's not what they remember here. John says the disciples recalled, "Zeal for Your house will consume Me." (John 2:17). That's about zeal for God's house. Nobody is resting in this courtyard anyway.

That sounds like a line from a psalm, and I can see why it came to mind. But the verse the disciples remember is, "Zeal for Your house will consume Me." (John 2:17). It's about zeal for God's house. Peace was not what was happening in those courts at that moment.

explanations.answer: A sign to prove His authority
explanations.explanation: That's right. The Jews demanded, "What sign can You show us to prove Your authority to do these things?" (John 2:18). They want proof for what He just did. Notice they ask for a sign, not an apology.

explanations.answer: A letter from the high priest
explanations.explanation: A letter would be very official, but nobody asks for one. The Jews demanded, "What sign can You show us to prove Your authority to do these things?" (John 2:18). They want a sign. Paperwork isn't mentioned.

explanations.answer: A record of His family line
explanations.explanation: A family record is a fair thing to want when you're checking someone out. But the text says they asked, "What sign can You show us to prove Your authority to do these things?" (John 2:18). It's a sign they want. His family tree never comes up.
Forty-six it is. The Jews say, "This temple took forty-six years to build" (John 2:20). That's a long time to build something. So hearing someone talk about three days sounds wild to them.

Seven is a number people love in the Bible, so I get it. But the Jews say, "This temple took forty-six years to build" (John 2:20). Seven years would be quick by comparison. Forty-six years is why three days sounds so impossible to them.

Twenty is a nice round number, but it's not the one in the verse. The Jews say, "This temple took forty-six years to build" (John 2:20). That's more than double. They're making the point that building takes a long time.
That's the twist, and you caught it. John tells us, "Jesus was speaking about the temple of His body." (John 2:21). The Jews heard a building. Jesus meant Himself.

Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, did build a temple (1 Kings 6:1). But that's not what Jesus meant. John says, "Jesus was speaking about the temple of His body." (John 2:21). The Jews took it the building way, and that's where the confusion came from.

Ezekiel, a prophet, did see a vision of a temple (Ezekiel 40:2). But John doesn't connect Jesus' words to it. He says, "Jesus was speaking about the temple of His body." (John 2:21). Jesus was talking about Himself.

explanations.answer: After He was raised from the dead
explanations.explanation: Right on time. John says, "After He was raised from the dead, His disciples remembered that He had said this." (John 2:22). The words didn't click in the moment. They did after the resurrection.

explanations.answer: On the walk back to Galilee
explanations.explanation: A long walk gives you time to think, so I see why you picked it. But John says the disciples remembered "After He was raised from the dead" (John 2:22). The walk isn't mentioned. The memory came after the resurrection.

explanations.answer: At the very next Passover Feast
explanations.explanation: That's a neat guess, but John doesn't say that. The text says the disciples remembered it "After He was raised from the dead" (John 2:22). Their remembering is tied to the resurrection, not a feast.
Believe is the word. John says many people saw the signs "and believed in His name." (John 2:23). The signs got their attention, and they believed. Keep that in mind for the next verse.
Prayer is good, but it's not in this verse. John says many people saw the signs "and believed in His name." (John 2:23). The word is believed. They saw something and put their trust in His name.
Gathering makes sense with a crowd at a feast. But John says many people saw the signs "and believed in His name." (John 2:23). The verse is about what they believed, not where they stood.

I get why you'd say that. If people believe in His name, you'd think He'd trust them back. But John says, "Jesus did not entrust Himself to them, for He knew them all." (John 2:24). So the answer is False.

False is right. John says, "Jesus did not entrust Himself to them, for He knew them all." (John 2:24). Many people believed in His name, yet He didn't entrust Himself to them. That's a surprise, and the text just tells us plainly.
That's the reason John gives. "Jesus did not entrust Himself to them, for He knew them all." (John 2:24). He didn't need anyone to explain people to Him. It's right there in the verse.

The feast was still going, friend. John says Jesus was in Jerusalem "at the Passover Feast" when many believed (John 2:23). The reason for not entrusting Himself is that "He knew them all." (John 2:24). Nothing there about the feast winding down.
That would make a good story, but John never says it. The reason he gives is, "He knew them all." (John 2:24). Verse 25 adds that He "did not need any testimony about man." Nobody had to warn Him.
